title: Working after school to pay for music lessons
summary: He did odd jobs to pay for lessons and clothes and practised anyway.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You worked your way. Didn't you work for your music lessons?

Yeah, well after I made my first communion I had made an oath that my mother and father would never have to buy me nothing. And I worked after school. I worked like all that area from Jackson, all over to Louisiana Avenue, and on the other side of St. Charles. Them white people, my people knew. All of us did that. My oldest sister, my oldest sister, Dr. Brun, which was one of the most Philippine, that's Philippine Britannia. And I worked on 3rd and Britannia, and I worked at a Hill Drug store right there in Washington,

The man liked me so much, I started there in school. And, no, when school was closed, I told him, we started going back to school. He said, well, you can come in after you come back to school. I worked until about, I closed up 11 or 12 o'clock. And I did yard-boy-wake, port-wake, little way to work and everything. I could go to work and other places on 7 and Coliseum. These are all rich people. My daddy knew it. My sister got jobs and everything. Them brothers got jobs and everything like that, you see. And that's why I said I paid my own music lessons and bought my own clothes and everything. When did you find time to practice? Huh?
When did you find time to practice? Oh, I found time to practice, yeah.

That was a must to me. Nobody had to tell me that, sure. But it must have been hard finding time if you were going to. Well, no, you were young and you were trying to make out you come from a poor family. I say poor, I mean we did have a place to sleep. We had to eat three meals a day and having a whole lot of clothes. Well, no, very few had the whole lot of clothes in those days. You know, you had maybe a suit, you called your son a suit, or you were going out a suit, a suit. Yeah. Then I got a job working for, let's see where the temple lay on it, or St. Charles and Padilla. My daddy was working there. He worked there a long time until he retired. St. Charles and Padilla. They had a cleaning place, a Howard cleaning place, right across from Beepin Shore. It's a spaghetti house now. And I was working there. When school closed, when school closed.

No, I wasn't working there when school was open. I don't think so. And I worked there. I had a place on Canal Street. I think it was a white jewelry store. Then I worked for Whirline, when Boerese, Miss Boerese had it. And after he found out my ability, he really knew Perkins, because Perkins used to come in the Groomwall store and had a Whirline store, which is still there. And I was supposed to run the elevator and help him behind the—keep stocks of all the things like strings and like things for the horns and everything. Then on the next floor, they had a repairman. Now, he was teaching me how to take a horn apart and put it in that asset and thing. And when school time comes, he was saying with me, my daddy demanded I go back to school. So I lost that job, you see. That was a pretty good paying job, you see. And if I knew about an instrument thing, I knew how to clean the violin, the shell over, string it up, put new strings on it and things like that. Wipe it off at the time, knew how to restock up the strings, all the string instruments for the read instruments and everything, you see. And most times in those days, the Whites and some of them Blacks, they couldn't read. I remember this drugstore, on the Hill Drugstore in Washington for times, they had, sometimes, a lot of white fellows couldn't read. They had a good memory. They had a few Whites. The man would get mad about them, tell them in front of us, say, you know, these fellows say, oh, I say, Magnus, he wasn't going to school, so why can't you read?
